Nike Inc. (NKE)

Historical Stock Performance Analysis — January 2000 to January 2026
Data Period: 2000-01-03 to 2026-01-30 • 6,559 trading days • Prices are split-adjusted • Source: Kaggle/NKE Historical Data

Executive Summary

Over a 26-year span from January 2000 to January 2026, Nike Inc. (NKE) delivered a cumulative return of 1282% (approximately a 13.8x multiple on invested capital), translating to a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 10.6%. An investor who purchased $10,000 of NKE on 2000-01-03 would hold approximately $138,235 by 2026-01-30.

The stock reached its all-time high of $166.25 on 2021-11-05. However, from that peak the stock experienced its largest drawdown of -68.5%, falling to $52.31 by 2025-04-08 — a decline that erased over a decade of gains. Annualized volatility over the full period was 31.2%, placing NKE in the higher-volatility tier for large-cap consumer stocks.

Nike's price history breaks into distinct phases: a deep decline in 2000 followed by a slow recovery through the mid-2000s, a sustained secular bull run from ~2009 to late 2021, and a sharp correction from late 2021 through the end of the dataset. Despite the recent drawdown, the long-term compounding record remains strong for patient holders who entered at earlier price levels.

Long-Term Price Trend Analysis

Nike's 26-year price chart tells a story of extraordinary long-term compounding punctuated by two major drawdowns. The chart below shows the split-adjusted closing price alongside 50-day and 200-day moving averages.

Phase I: The Early-2000s Decline (2000–2002)

NKE entered the dataset at approximately $4.47 (split-adjusted) in January 2000 and quickly plunged to an all-time low of $2.47 on 2000-02-25 — a decline of roughly -45% in under two months. This corresponded with the broader dot-com bust and Nike-specific headwinds. The stock remained depressed through much of 2000–2002, trading below $5 for extended periods.

Phase II: Recovery and Steady Growth (2003–2008)

From the 2000–2002 lows, Nike entered a sustained recovery. The stock climbed steadily through the mid-2000s, benefiting from strong brand momentum and international expansion. By late 2007, NKE was trading in the $15–$17 range — a more than 5x recovery from the early-decade trough. The 2008 Global Financial Crisis interrupted this run, pulling the stock back to the ~$9–$10 area, but the drawdown was comparatively contained relative to the broader market.

Phase III: The Secular Bull Run (2009–2021)

Post-GFC marked the beginning of Nike's most powerful growth phase. Fueled by the Direct-to-Consumer (DTC) transformation, digital strategy acceleration, and global athletic wear tailwinds, NKE compounded relentlessly for over a decade. The stock broke $50 in 2018, $100 in 2020, and reached its all-time high of $166.25 on 2021-11-05. This 12-year run delivered roughly a 16x return from the GFC lows.

Phase IV: The Post-Peak Correction (2021–2026)

Following the November 2021 peak, NKE entered a protracted decline that accelerated through 2024 and into 2025. By 2025-04-08, the stock had fallen to $52.31 — a -68.5% peak-to-trough drawdown, the deepest in the dataset. This correction reflected multiple headwinds: increased competition, DTC strategy recalibration, inventory challenges, and a rotation away from pandemic-era consumer discretionary winners. As of 2026-01-30, NKE closed at $61.81, still well below its all-time high.

Key Observation: The 2021–2025 drawdown of -68.5% is the largest in Nike's 26-year history in this dataset, exceeding even the early-2000s decline and the 2008 GFC pullback. This underscores the valuation risk inherent in buying at peak multiples.

Volatility and Risk Assessment

Nike's annualized volatility over the full period stands at 31.2%, meaningfully above the ~15–20% range typical of large-cap consumer staples but in line with higher-beta consumer discretionary names. Volatility has not been constant — it has clustered around major market dislocations and company-specific events.

The 30-day rolling volatility (blue) captures short-term spikes, while the 252-day measure (orange) reveals the structural volatility regime. Major spikes are visible during:

  • Early 2000: Extreme 30-day volatility exceeding 80% during the rapid sell-off
  • 2008–2009: Elevated volatility through the financial crisis, with 30-day readings above 50%
  • March 2020: COVID-19 shock produced a sharp volatility spike
  • 2024–2025: Sustained elevated volatility during the ongoing correction

Intraday Range

The 30-day average intraday range (High–Low as a percentage of Close) confirms the same volatility clustering pattern.

Trading Volume Patterns

Average daily trading volume across the full period was 10.7 million shares. Volume patterns have evolved significantly over time, both due to structural market changes (decimalization, algorithmic trading) and Nike-specific catalysts.

The overlay chart reveals several key patterns:

  • Volume-price correlation during sell-offs: The sharpest volume spikes coincide with rapid price declines — notably early 2000, 2008, and the 2024–2025 correction — indicating capitulation-type selling.
  • Secular volume trends: Volume was elevated in the early 2000s, moderated during the steady mid-2010s advance, and rose again during the post-2021 volatility.
  • Breakout confirmation: The transition from accumulation to advance in 2009–2010 was accompanied by rising volume, lending technical credibility to the bull phase.

Key Takeaways and Investment Implications

1. Proven Long-Term Compounder with High Entry-Point Sensitivity

NKE's 10.6% CAGR and 1282% cumulative return over 26 years confirm it as a strong long-term compounder. However, the severity of the post-2021 drawdown (-68.5%) illustrates that when you buy matters enormously — even for blue-chip names. Investors who entered at the November 2021 peak have experienced devastating capital loss.

2. Volatility Is Higher Than Perception Suggests

At 31.2% annualized volatility, NKE is significantly more volatile than many investors expect for a mega-cap consumer brand. This volatility has been persistent across eras, not just concentrated in crisis periods. Position sizing should reflect this risk.

3. Drawdown Duration Is the Hidden Risk

The top drawdown episodes show durations spanning years, not months. The current drawdown from the 2021 peak has lasted over three years with no full recovery. Long-term compounding requires surviving — psychologically and financially — these extended underwater periods.

4. Volume Signals Are Informative

Volume spikes have historically been reliable markers of capitulation events. The highest-volume days are disproportionately associated with sharp declines, suggesting they may represent contrarian entry opportunities on longer timeframes.

5. Decade-Level Dispersion Is Extreme

The difference between Nike's best and worst decades is dramatic. The 2010s delivered exceptional returns with contained risk, while the 2000s and 2020s have tested investor patience. This dispersion underscores the importance of understanding the business cycle and competitive positioning — not just buying and holding blindly.

Investor Conclusion: Nike's historical record supports a thesis of high-quality compounding, but the asset demands discipline around entry valuation, tolerance for extended drawdowns, and a truly long-term horizon. The current drawdown from all-time highs may present an opportunity for patient capital — or signal a structural de-rating. The data alone cannot resolve this forward-looking question, but it provides the essential backdrop for framing it.
